To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The dominant framing of adaptation as a national and sub-national issue has been challenged by the recognition of borderless climate impacts, which cascade through the international and regional system, in simple or complex ways.
the territorial framing of climate change adaptation has become dominant because of the epistemic and institutional features of adaptation science and governance.

a territorial framing of adaptation is reinforced by an epistemic community of adaptation experts that is based on a strong environmental science foundation and a reliance on place based research and by the international norm of national responsibility for adaptation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the territorial framing of climate change impacts and adaptation is being challenged by "borderless climate risk" and how this is being reflected in governance responses.
the governance of cross border climate risks and the ways in which the international system can contribute to reducing vulnerability.
the role of the nation state and its international system in shaping adaptation governance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the territorial framing is not sufficient to address borderless climate risks.
the international system is not well equipped to deal with borderless climate risks.

the territorial framing of climate risks has been dominant in adaptation governance and that the notion of border less climate risks challenges this framing, but that the governance responses to this challenge are only just emerging.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the territorial framing of climate change adaptation is a powerful and persistent feature of the problem structure that has been reinforced by the international norm of national or local responsibility.
the territorial framing of climate change risks is not only a problem for climate change adaptation, but also a problem for climate governance more broadly.

the territorial framing of climate change adaptation has been reinforced by the international norm of national and sub national responsibility for adaptation, and that this has limited the development of governance responses that could address borderless climate risks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IR community should be more engaged in the study of climate adaptation governance.
the territorial framing of climate risks is a product of the epistemic communities that interpret them, as well as the norms and rules that govern the international climate change regime.
the territorial framing of climate change adaptation is not a given, and we should consider how to govern borderless climate risks in the future.
